Its range is relatively high, and the sound is sharp and strongly rhythmic. A stroke produces a sound that decays quickly, without long resonance, yet its distinctive clang stands out in a band. Compared with the low, heavy sound of drums, the cowbell is lighter and more nimble; compared with a gong or bell, it is sharper and more exciting, without a deep resonant foundation. Its sound is marked by having no definite pitch, and the natural resonance of the metal produces its particular acoustic effect; in Latin music and pop it is often used to strengthen the sense of rhythm and to build a cheerful atmosphere.

The cowbell is a hand-struck idiophone, H-S number 111.242.11, whose name comes from the bell herdsmen hung on cattle to identify them. It is traditionally of metal, and modern ones may be of synthetic material. Tuned cowbells are mostly brass bell bodies that keep the metal clapper; the clapperless cowbell is struck with a beater at different points, and the holding hand damps it to change the timbre, and it can also be played with a converted bass-drum pedal or with a double-bass bow. It is used in Latin, rock, Cuban and Caribbean music, and also appears in Alpine performance, classical music and cheering at sporting events.
牛鈴為體鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 111.242.11，基: The cowbell is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.242.11, with Europe given as its basic region. Traditionally it is made of metal, and some modern variants use synthetic materials. Tuned cowbells (Almglocken) are usually spherical brass bells that keep a metal clapper; the clapperless cowbell is also of metal and is struck with a stick. A cylindrical wooden block played in the same way is also called agogô. The source does not state the materials of the other parts, such as the beater, the means of holding it, the pedal or the bow.
牛鈴為體鳴樂器，演奏時一手持握鈴體，另一手持鼓棒敲擊；音色可透過敲擊不同部位與手: The cowbell is an idiophone, played with the bell held in one hand and struck with a stick in the other; the timbre can be changed by striking different points and damping with the palm. A set of several bells can be struck one by one or against each other, and it can also be played with the foot on a converted bass-drum pedal, or bowed with a double-bass bow. A beginner should first hold the bell steadily and control the striking point and the sustain, then practise rhythmic changes between the different bell positions.
牛鈴見於拉丁、搖滾、拉丁美洲與哥哥音樂。無舌牛鈴以鼓棒敲擊，古巴音樂稱 cenc: The cowbell appears in Latin, rock, Latin American and go-go music. The clapperless cowbell is struck with a drumstick; in Cuban music it is called the cencerro and is often played by the same person as the bongo drums; in Caribbean music two or three can be mounted together with the timbales. The tuned cowbell has also entered classical music, for example Richard Strauss's Alpine Symphony; Olivier Messiaen uses sets of clapperless cowbells in Et expecto resurrectionem mortuorum and Couleurs de la cité céleste.
牛鈴起源於牧場，牧人將鈴掛在動物頸部以辨識位置，因牛使用廣泛而得名。早期與傳統為: The cowbell began in the pasture, where herdsmen hung bells on animals to know where they were, and it takes its name from its wide use on cattle. Early and traditional ones are of metal, and modern ones may be of synthetic material. The clapperless metal cowbell is an important element of Latin American music and go-go music; in West Africa they come in pairs or sets of three, in Brazil the instrument is called agogô, in Cuba cencerro, and in the Caribbean it is mounted together with the timbales. Tuned cowbells are used in tourism in the northern Alps and in classical music, as in Richard Strauss's Alpine Symphony. The sports noisemaker may traditionally go back to nineteenth-century baseball played in cattle pastures, and it later spread to many other sports; Mississippi State University and the Southeastern Conference changed their rules in 2010 and 2014.
